ex.ja: もし電話がなければ、不便だろう。

Compellingly attractive.

Coloured a brilliant turquoise.

mermaid.ety: From Middle English mermayde (“maid of the sea”), from mere (“sea, lake”) + maid, equivalent to mer- + maid. ex.ja: ボブは自分の力でこの厳しい試練を乗り切らねばいけない。

shire.ety:

ex.ja: 私の目は強い日光を浴びて細くなった。

note.ja: ラテン語 poena（罰）から。「刑罰の」。penalty、pain と同じ。

The labia (majora).
To spread out from, like the petals of a flower

ex.en: Petals lie on the surface of the water.
ex.ja: 花びらが水面に浮かんでいる。

ex.en: The petals of this rose are very tender.
ex.ja: このバラの花びらはとても柔らかい。

ex.en: The petals are floating on the water.
ex.ja: 花びらが水面に浮かんでいる。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 petalon（葉）から。petalos（広がった）。「花びら」。

en: A flat piece of wood on which to cook fish, so that the wood provides flavor and helps to produce a pleasing texture.
An object made of planks; planking.
To cover something with planking.
To bake (fish, etc.) on a piece of cedar lumber.

plank.ety: From Middle English plank, planke, borrowed from Old French planke, Old Northern French planque (compare French planche, from Old French planche), from Vulgar Latin planca, from palanca, from Latin phalanga. The Latin term derives from the Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), so it is thus a doublet of phalange and phalanx. Compare also the doublets planch, planche, and plancha, borrowed later from Middle French, Modern French, and Spanish, respectively.

ex.en: He upped one end of the plank.
ex.ja: 彼は板の片端を持ち上げた。

ex.en: The plank froze to the ground.
ex.ja: 板は地面に凍りついた。

ex.en: He hammered nails into the plank.
ex.ja: 板にくぎを打ち込んだ。

note.ja: ラテン語 planca（厚板）から。「厚板」→ 政策の土台の板 →「政策の柱」。

en: A dire or unfortunate situation.
Specifically, to pledge (one's troth etc.) as part of a marriage ceremony.
To promise (oneself) to someone, or to do something.

plight.ety: From Middle English plit (“fold, wrinkle, bad situation”), conflation of Middle English pliht, plight (“risky promise, peril”) (from Old English pliht "danger, risk"; see Etymology 2) and Anglo-Norman plit, plyte (“fold, condition”), from Old French pleit (“condition, manner of folding”) (from Vulgar Latin *plictum, from Latin plicitum (“fold”)).

ex.ja: 裁判長は被告に大いに同情していた。

en: Private, exclusive; not public; one's own.
With knowledge of; party to; let in on.
An outdoor facility for urination and defecation, whether open (latrine) or enclosed (outhouse).
A lavatory: a room with a toilet.

privy.ety: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”). Doublet of private.

en: The process of propelling, driving, or pushing, typically forward or onward; a propulsive force or impulse.
That which propels.

propulsion.ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

note.ja: pro（前へ）+ puls（押す）+ ion。前へ押し出すこと →「推進（力）」。propel（推進する）。

en: A flat-bottomed craft able to float and drift on water, used for transport or as a waterborne platform.
Any flattish thing, usually wooden, used in a similar fashion.
To convey on a raft.
To make into a raft.

raft.ety: Late Middle English, of North Germanic origin, from West Old Norse raptr, from Proto-Germanic *raf-tra-, from Proto-Indo-European *rap-tro-, from *rep- (“stake, beam”). See also Norwegian raft (“beam, rafter”), Danish raft (“thin pole”). Compare also Albanian trap (“raft, ferry”).

ex.en: Tom went down the river on a raft.
ex.ja: トムは、いかだで川を下った。

ex.en: The boys went down the river on a raft.
ex.ja: 少年たちはいかだで川をくだった。

ex.en: He crossed the immense pacific on a raft.
ex.ja: 彼は広大な太平洋をいかだで横断した。

note.ja: 北欧語 raptr（丸太）から。「いかだ」。「大量（a raft of）」は別系統とされる。

en: To be very happy, be delighted, exult; to feel joy.
To make happy, exhilarate.

rejoice.ety: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Doublet of rejoy. Compare French réjouir; Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire

ex.en: They rejoiced over the news of our success.
ex.ja: 彼らは我々の成功の知らせを喜んだ。

ex.en: They rejoiced when they heard he was safe.
ex.ja: 彼が無事だと聞いて彼らは喜んだ。

ex.en: We have rejoiced over his discovery.
ex.ja: 私たちは彼の発見を喜んだ。

note.ja: re（強意）+ joir（喜ぶ）。ラテン語 gaudere（喜ぶ）。joy と同じ。

en: That which remains; that which is left after loss or decay; a remaining portion.
Something old and outdated, possibly kept for sentimental reasons.
To cause (an object) to appear old or worn, to distress.
Pertaining to the Big Bang.

relic.ety: From Middle English relik et al., from Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae (“remains, relics”), from relinquō (“to leave behind, abandon, relinquish”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”). Doublet of relict, derelict, and relinquish.

ex.en: Here were some relics.
ex.ja: ここにいくつかの遺跡がありました。

ex.en: We discovered relics of an ancient civilization.
ex.ja: 我々は古代文明の遺跡を発見した。

ex.en: Rome abounds with relics.
ex.ja: ローマは至る所に遺跡がある。

note.ja: ラテン語 reliquiae（残り物）から。re + linquere（残す）。「遺物・遺品」。relinquish（放棄する）と同じ。

en: To wander or travel freely and with no specific destination.
To range or wander over.
The act of roaming; a wander; a travel without aim or destination

roam.ety: From Middle English romen, from Old English rāmian, from Proto-Germanic *raimōną (“to wander”), from *raim- (“to move, raise”), from *h₃reyH- (“to move, lift, flow”). Akin to Old English ārǣman (“to arise, stand up, lift up”), Old High German rāmēn (“to aim”) ( > archaic German rahmen (“to strive”)), Middle Dutch rammen (“to night-wander, to copulate”), rammelen (“to wander about, ramble”). More at ramble.

ex.en: His eyes roamed over the lake in the valley.
ex.ja: 彼の目は谷間の湖上をずっとさまよった。

ex.en: I like to roam about the fields.
ex.ja: 私は野原を歩き回るのが好きだ。

ex.en: They roamed about the forest.
ex.ja: 彼らは森を歩き回った。

note.ja: 中英語 romen から。語源ははっきりしない。「歩き回る」。roaming。

en: A type of open shoe made up of straps or bands holding a sole to the foot
To put on sandals.

sandal.ety: From Middle English sandal (“sandal”), from Old French sandale, from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”), of unknown origin. Often mistakenly parsed as related to sand.

ex.en: I bought a pair of sandals that match him.
ex.ja: 彼とお揃いのサンダルを買ったの。

ex.en: I bought a pair of sandals.
ex.ja: サンダルを買った。

ex.en: I forgot to bring sandals.
ex.ja: サンダル、持ってくるの忘れちゃった。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 sandalon から。ペルシャ語に由来するとされる。

en: A snake-like creature, such as a sea serpent.
A person who is subtle, malicious, treacherous, or deceiving.

From Middle English serpent, from Old French serpent (“snake, serpent”), from Latin serpēns (“snake”), present active participle of serpere (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Italic *serpō, from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. In this sense, displaced native Old English nǣdre (“snake, serpent”), whence Modern English adder.
Compare Sanskrit सर्प (sarpa, “snake”), which is a descendant of the same Proto-Indo-European word as

note.ja: ラテン語 serpens（這うもの）から。serpere（這う）。「大きなヘビ」。

en: A tropical Asian plant (Sesamum indicum) bearing small flat seeds used as food and as a source of oil.
The seed of this plant.

sesame.ety: From late Middle English sisamie, from Latin sīsamum, sēsamum, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon), from Aramaic שושמא (šūššmā), shortening of שומשומא (šumššumā), from Akkadian 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈬 (šamaššammū, “oil plant”), compound of 𒉌𒄑 (šaman, “oil”) and 𒌑 (šammum, “plant”). The modern pronunciation is perhaps influenced by (transliterations of) Greek σησάμη (sisámi). Doublet of sesamum.

ex.en: I want to eat a black sesame ice cream.
ex.ja: 黒ごまのアイスクリームを食べたいよ。

ex.en: I ate black sesame ice cream.
ex.ja: 僕は黒ゴマのアイスクリームを食べました。

ex.en: I want to know how to make black sesame tofu.
ex.ja: 黒ごま豆腐の作り方が知りたい。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 sēsamon から。セム語系の言葉に由来する。Open sesame（開けゴマ）は『アラビアンナイト』から。

en: To push, especially roughly or with force.
To move off or along by an act of pushing, as with an oar or pole used in a boat; sometimes with off.
A rough push.
A forward movement of packed river-ice.

shove.ety:
From Middle English schouven, from Old English sċūfan, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuban, from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ-.
See also West Frisian skowe, Low German schuven, Dutch schuiven, German schieben, Danish skubbe, Norwegian Bokmål skyve, Norwegian Nynorsk skuva; also Lithuanian skùbti (“to hurry”), Polish skubać (“to pluck”), Albanian humb (“to lose”).

ex.en: He shoved the letter into his pocket.
ex.ja: 彼は手紙をポケットにねじ込んだ。

ex.en: The man shoved her aside.
ex.ja: その男は彼女を押しのけた。

ex.en: I shoved my hands into my pockets.
ex.ja: 私はポケットに手を突っ込んだ。

note.ja: 古英語 scūfan（押す）から。shovel と同系。「乱暴に押す」。

en: To make simpler, either by reducing in complexity, reducing to component parts, or making easier to understand.
To become simpler.

simplify.ety: From the French simplifier, equivalent to simple + -ify.

ex.en: A good writer needs to be able to simplify complicated things.
ex.ja: 優れた作家は、複雑なものを単純化できる必要があるのです。

ex.en: Simplify your life. Take advice from native speakers.
ex.ja: 人生を楽にせよ。母語話者からの助言を受け入れよ。

note.ja: simpl（単純な）+ ify（〜にする）。単純にする →「簡単にする・単純化する」。

en: One of a group of nymphs who lured mariners to their death on the rocks.
One who sings sweetly and charms.
To make a noise with, or as if with, a siren.
To drive with a siren on.
Relating to or like a siren.

siren.ety: From Middle English siren, from Old French sereine and Latin Sīrēn, Sīrēna, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). The mammalian sense was first attested in French in Dominique Bouhours, Les entretiens d'Ariste et d'Eugène, in 1671. The aquatic salamander sense was originally introduced by Linnaeus in 1766, for a genus of his reptiles.

ex.en: I heard sirens in the distance.
ex.ja: 遠くにあるサイレンの音が聞こえてきた。

ex.en: I heard a siren.
ex.ja: サイレンが聞こえてきた。

ex.en: The siren sounded an emergency.
ex.ja: サイレンが急変を知らせました。

note.ja: ギリシャ神話で歌声で船乗りを惑わすセイレーン（Seirēn）から。人を引きつける音 →「サイレン」。

ja: （ヒット作に化けた）意外な作品

en: Someone who sleeps.
That which lies dormant, as a law.

sleeper.ety: From Middle English sleper, equivalent to sleep + -er.

ex.en: I'm a light sleeper.
ex.ja: 眠りが浅いんだ。

ex.en: As one grows old, one becomes a light sleeper.
ex.ja: 年を取ると目ざとくなる。

en: To spread (a substance, especially one that colours or is dirty) across a surface by rubbing.
To cover (a surface with a layer of some substance) by rubbing.
A mark made by smearing.
A presentation of a sauce, purée or other food item, which is placed in a dollop and spread across the plate.

smear.ety:
From Middle English smeren, smerien, from Old English smerian, smyrian, smierwan (“to anoint or rub with grease, oil, etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *smirwijan, from Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną. Doublet of schmear.
Cognate with Saterland Frisian smeere, Dutch smeren (“to smear, lubricate”), Low German smeren, German schmieren (“to smear, lubricate”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål smøre (“to lubricate”), Norwegian Nynorsk smørja (“to lubricate”), Swedish smörja (“to grease”), Faroese and Icelandic smyrja.

ex.en: I'd like to have a Pap smear done.
ex.ja: 子宮癌の検査をしていただきたいのです。

ex.en: The ruling party is running a smear campaign against the opposition.
ex.ja: 与党は野党非難のキャンペーンを展開しています。

note.ja: 古英語 smierwan（油を塗る）から。「塗りつける」→（評判を）汚す →「中傷する」。

en: Marked by snow; characterized by snow.
Covered with snow; snow-covered; besnowed.
Synonym of snowy owl.
Synonym of snowy egret.

snowy.ety: From Middle English snowy, snawy; from Old English snāwiġ. By surface analysis, snow + -y.

ex.en: As the weather was snowy, we went skiing.
ex.ja: 雪の降る天気だったので、私たちはスキーに行った。

ex.ja: 雪降りの日です。

ex.en: According to the weather forecast, tomorrow will be snowy.
ex.ja: 天気予報によればあすは雪だ。

The petiole, pedicel, or peduncle of a plant.

To (try to) follow or contact someone constantly, often resulting in harassment.ᵂᵖ

ex.en: The stalk is a little bigger around than your little finger.
ex.ja: その茎は君の小指よりやや太い。

ex.en: Wash the strawberries and remove their stalks.
ex.ja: イチゴを洗って、ヘタを取って。

ex.en: Oh, the rice stalk is sticking up in the tea. Something good might happen.
ex.ja: あ、茶柱が立ってる。何かいいこと起きるかも。

note.ja: 「茎」は古英語 stela から。「忍び寄る」は古英語 stealcian（こっそり歩く）からで別語、steal と同系。

en: A man who is a leader in national or international affairs.
A male political leader who promotes the public good or who is recognized for probity, leadership, or the qualities necessary to govern a…

statesman.ety: From state + -s- + -man, modelled after French homme d'État.

ex.en: He is as great a statesman as any.
ex.ja: 彼は世にもまれな大政治家である。

ex.en: The newspaper reported the death of the statesman.
ex.ja: 新聞はその政治家の死を報道した。

ex.en: The great statesman and general is still living.
ex.ja: 偉大な政治家でもあり将軍である人はまだ生きている。

note.ja: state（国家）+ s + man。「国家の人」→「（立派な）政治家」。

en: To have a strong bad smell.
To be greatly inferior; to perform badly.
A strong bad smell.
A complaint or objection.
Bad-smelling, stinky.

stink.ety:
From Middle English stinken, from Old English stincan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *stengʷ-, *stegʷ- (“to push, thrust, strike”). Cognate with West Frisian stjonke (“to stink”), Dutch stinken (“to stink”), German stinken (“to stink”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk stinke (“to stink”), Swedish stinka (“to stink”), Icelandic stökkva (“to spring, leap, jump”).
Compare typologically Russian рази́ть (razítʹ).

ex.en: Durian stinks, but it's said to be very healthy.
ex.ja: ドリアンは臭いけど、体にはとてもいいと言われています。

ex.en: I'll bid farewell to this stinking school.
ex.ja: このひどい学校にはおさらばだ。

ex.en: He is raising a big stink over a minor glitch.
ex.ja: 彼はささいな故障に大騒ぎをしています。

note.ja: 古英語 stincan（においがする）から。「悪臭を放つ」。stench と同じ。

en: Of or pertaining to storms.
Characterized by, or proceeding from, a storm; subject to storms; agitated with strong winds and heavy rain.

stormy.ety: From Middle English stormy, stormi, from Old English *stormiġ (“stormy”), equivalent to storm + -y. Cognate with Dutch stormig (“stormy”), German stürmisch (“stormy”), Swedish stormig (“stormy”).

ex.en: I hope this stormy weather won't go on.
ex.ja: この嵐が続かなければいいのですが。

ex.en: There is a risk that it may become stormy.
ex.ja: 嵐になる恐れがあります。

ex.en: It was stormy the day before yesterday.
ex.ja: おとといは嵐だった。

note.ja: storm（嵐）+ -y。「嵐の・激しい」。

ex.ja: 結局これでは駄目だとだけ言っておこう。

ex.ja: 今のところそれで間に合うでしょう。

ex.ja: 言うまでもなく、エドナはなにもできない。

note.ja: symbol（象徴）+ -ism。「象徴性・象徴主義」。

Intricate.

tram.ety:
Early 16th century, borrowed from Scots, probably from Low German traam (“tram, shaft of a barrow”), from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch trame (“narrow shaft, beam”), said to be ultimately from a lost West Germanic (Ingvaeonic) word, probably from Proto-Germanic *drum (“splinter, fragment”), from Proto-Indo-European *térmn̥ (“peg, post, boundary”), cognate with Latin terminus.
Compare Middle Low German treme; West Flemish traam, trame.
The popular derivation from the surname of the English pioneer tramway builder Benjamin Outram (1764–1805) is false: the term pre-dated him.

First English attestation dates to 1587 (OED).

note.ja: aud（聞く）+ ible（〜できる）。聞くことができる →「聞こえる」。inaudible（聞こえない）。
